headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Child and Adolescent Pregnancy
headings.content: Child and adolescent pregnancy refers to any pregnancy in a girl aged 10 to 19 years old. In global health and Nigerian clinical practice, this demographic is further split into early adolescence (10 to 14 years) and late adolescence (15 to 19 years). Pregnancies in the younger age group carry exponentially higher risks due to ongoing physical immaturity. Midwives and nurses in primary health centers often encounter these cases, making a clear understanding of the age classifications vital for immediate risk stratification and appropriate referrals.

headings.title: Biological and Physiological Immaturity
headings.content:
The female adolescent body is often unready for the physical demands of gestation and childbearing. 

- **Pelvic development**: The bony pelvis continues to grow for several years after menarche. A narrow, underdeveloped pelvic brim increases the likelihood of cephalopelvic disproportion.
- **Uterine vascularization**: Uterine blood flow and muscular development may be suboptimal, restricting fetal nutrient exchange.
- **Nutritional competition**: A growing teenager and a developing fetus compete directly for essential micronutrients like iron, calcium, and folate, impairing growth for both.
- **Hormonal axis**: Endocrine immaturity can lead to irregular ovulatory cycles and higher rates of spontaneous abortion.

headings.title: Contributing Factors and Social Determinants
headings.content: Adolescent pregnancy rarely happens in isolation; it is driven by a complex web of socioeconomic factors. Poverty stands out as a primary catalyst, often forcing young girls out of school and limiting their access to reproductive health information. Cultural practices, early marriages, peer pressure, and limited availability of youth-friendly contraceptive services further compound the vulnerability. Gender inequality and sexual coercion also expose young females to unprotected intercourse against their will.

headings.title: Physical and Psychological Risks for Young Mothers
headings.content: The physical toll of carrying a pregnancy to term during adolescence includes severe conditions such as pregnancy-induced hypertension, severe anemia, and obstructed labor. The risk of obstetric fistulas—abnormal openings between the vagina and the bladder or rectum—is particularly high due to prolonged pressure on soft tissues in an unconditioned pelvis. Psychologically, young mothers face profound social stigma, depression, anxiety, and a disruption of their educational and economic trajectory.

headings.title: Fetal and Neonatal Complications
headings.content: Babies born to adolescent mothers experience adverse outcomes at much higher rates than those born to adult women. Low birth weight is common, largely driven by intrauterine growth restriction and preterm delivery. Neonatal mortality rates are elevated, and surviving infants may experience developmental delays or chronic nutritional deficits. The immature physiological state of the mother fails to provide an optimal intrauterine environment.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Antenatal Care
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment for pregnant adolescents goes beyond routine vital signs. Nurses must evaluate nutritional status, screen for domestic violence, assess mental health status, and build a trusting, non-judgmental rapport. Antenatal visits should offer education on danger signs, nutritional counseling with iron and folate supplementation, and birth preparedness plans. Early booking in the antenatal clinic remains the bedrock for preventing adverse outcomes.

headings.title: Intrapartum and Postpartum Nursing Management
headings.content: During labor and delivery, close monitoring is essential. Nurses should use the partograph diligently to detect prolonged labor early. Emotional support from a birth companion helps reduce anxiety. Postpartum care focuses on monitoring for postpartum hemorrhage, preventing infection, and promoting bonding and breastfeeding. Providing contraception counseling before discharge is vital to prevent rapid repeat pregnancies.

headings.title: Prevention, Counseling, and Community Support
headings.content: Addressing adolescent pregnancy requires multi-sectoral community intervention. Nurses play a major role in school health education, community outreach, and advocating for girl-child education. Providing youth-friendly sexual health services empowers teenagers to make informed decisions. Engaging community leaders and parents helps dismantle cultural stigmas while encouraging supportive networks for young mothers who choose to return to school.
